content: Cimicifuga racemosa, also known as Black cohosh, Black bugbane, Black snakeroot, or Fairy candle (synonym: Actaea racemosa), is a plant belonging to the Ranunculaceae family. It is native to eastern North America, ranging from southern Ontario to central Georgia and extending westward to Missouri and Arkansas. This plant thrives in various woodland environments and is often found in small woodland clearings. The plant can grow up to 2 meters (approximately 7 feet) tall. Its basal leaves are large, reaching up to 1 meter (39 inches) in length and width, and are tripinnately compound with coarsely toothed margins. The flowers are arranged in racemes that can grow up to 50 cm (20 inches) long. These flowers lack petals and sepals but feature a dense cluster of 55–110 white stamens, each 5–10 mm long, surrounding a white stigma. The flowers emit a distinctly sweet fragrance. The fruit is a dry follicle, 5–10 mm long, containing several seeds. It is important to note that Blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), despite its similar name, belongs to a different genus. Herbal Use Black cohosh has been included in herbal remedies and dietary supplements marketed to women for alleviating symptoms of premenstrual tension, menopause, and other gynecological issues. However, a study published in the Annals of Medicine (December 19, 2006) raised significant doubts about its efficacy. The study found that Black cohosh was slightly less effective than a placebo and concluded that the herb shows little potential as an important therapy for relief of vasomotor symptoms. Notably, the study used a product containing 5 mg of the active component daily, whereas the standard long-used product, Remifemin, contains 2 mg per day. The American Botanical Council has discussed this study in detail. It was previously believed that Black cohosh contained estrogen-like compounds, but recent research suggests that its effects may be mediated through binding to serotonin receptors. Historically, Native Americans used Black cohosh to treat gynecological disorders, sore throats, kidney problems, and even depression. It has also been used as an abortifacient. Side Effects Black cohosh should not be used during pregnancy or lactation. There is a documented case of neurological complications in a post-term baby following labor induction with a mixture of Black cohosh and Blue cohosh during a home birth. Other adverse outcomes in neonates born to women who reportedly used Blue cohosh to induce labor have been published in peer-reviewed journals. Black cohosh stimulates the endometrium and increases blood flow to the pelvic area. Its use is not recommended during menstruation, as it may increase or prolong bleeding. Due to its potential estrogenic effects, it should be used cautiously for no longer than six months. Additionally, Black cohosh contains tannin, which inhibits iron absorption. This, combined with its potential to enhance menstrual bleeding, warrants monitoring of iron levels during its use. No long-term safety studies in humans have been published. Concerns exist that, due to its estrogen-like effects, prolonged use may promote metastasis of estrogen-sensitive cancer tissues by stimulating cells in the endometrium or breast. In an unpublished experiment on mice, Black cohosh increased metastasis of cancer to the lungs, although it did not increase the incidence of breast cancer. The lung tumors in this study were observed but not biopsied. There have been reports of severe liver damage in a few individuals using Black cohosh. However, many women have taken the herb for years without reporting adverse health effects. Australia has added a warning to the labels of all Black cohosh products, stating that it may harm the liver in some individuals and should not be used without medical supervision. Aside from pregnancy-related complications, increased menstrual bleeding, anemia, and rare but serious hepatic dysfunction, reported side effects include dizziness, diarrhea, nausea, and occasional gastric discomfort. Other possible side effects include headaches, seizures, vomiting, sweating, constipation, low blood pressure, slow heartbeats, and weight changes. Garden Use Cimicifuga racemosa grows well in consistently moist, relatively heavy soil. It produces tall, tapering racemes of white midsummer flowers on wiry black-purple stems. These flowers have a mildly unpleasant, medicinal smell at close range, which gives the plant its common name, Bugbane. The drying seed heads remain visually appealing in the garden for many weeks. Its burgundy, deeply cut leaves add aesthetic interest to American gardens, particularly in areas where summer heat and drought do not cause the plant to die back. This makes it a popular perennial for gardens.
